label: sql-cte-recursive-hierarchy-en
top_ai_sentences:
Recursive CTEs, on the other hand, are
part of the SQL standard.

The syntax is similar across engines; some require the RECURSIVE
keyword, and some don't (SQL Server, for example).
SQL Server users can override the default limit of 100 with OPTION (MAXRECURSION N).

It makes debugging easier and gives you a simple way to cap
  recursion.

It's got an anchor member (the base case) and a recursive
member (the part that joins back to the CTE).
Using UNION instead of UNION ALL for no reason.

It's got two moving parts: an anchor member that picks the starting rows, and a
recursive member that joins those rows back to the source table.

Recursive CTEs don't support cycle detection natively, so you've got to build
that part yourself.
For a deeper guide, see [Transform Data in the Warehouse with dbt](/recipes/python-dbt-model-transformations/).
Add a safety limit such as WHERE depth < N to prevent infinite recursion on cyclic data.
For simple trees without cycles, yes.
A recursive CTE is one that references itself.
Use a recursive CTE when you need to walk a hierarchy from a known starting point.
Always include a depth or level column.

The database evaluates the anchor first, then keeps applying the
recursive member until it stops producing new rows.
Build a path column for debugging so you can see the exact traversal route.

CONNECT BY is more concise but less flexible, so use recursive CTEs when you care
about portability.
Test with small datasets first; recursive CTEs can be slow on large tables.

Without a starting point the CTE returns nothing; the anchor has to select rows
  that don't depend on the CTE.

Add a depth limit such as WHERE depth < 100, or track visited nodes in a path array or string and check for
repeats.

Most modern SQL engines support them: PostgreSQL, MySQL 8.0+, SQLite 3.8.4+, SQL Server (2008+), Oracle
(11gR2+), Snowflake, BigQuery, and DuckDB.

UNION deduplicates results and adds overhead, so use
  UNION ALL unless you actually need deduplication.
CONNECT BY is Oracle's proprietary syntax, also supported by Snowflake.
Recursive CTEs return depth-first by default.

Use ORDER BY depth if you want
  breadth-first output.

top_ai_sentences: Ayuda a debuggear y te da una forma fácil de limitar la recursión.
Es una CTE que se referencia a sí misma.

Para grafos con ciclos o problemas de shortest path, usá una graph database
o un algoritmo especializado.
Saltearse la detección de ciclos.

Las CTEs recursivas son el
estándar SQL.

Sin un punto de partida la CTE no retorna nada; el anchor tiene que seleccionar filas
  que no dependan de la CTE.

La sintaxis es similar en todos; algunos requieren el keyword RECURSIVE, y otros no (por ejemplo SQL
Server).
Para una guía más profunda, consultá [Transform Data in the Warehouse with dbt](/es/recipes/python-dbt-model-transformations/).

Una Common Table Expression (CTE) recursiva permite que una query se referencie a sí misma, así podés recorrer
datos jerárquicos almacenados en una sola tabla.
Para árboles simples sin ciclos, sí.

El join recursivo hace JOIN c ON c.parent_id = h.id; sin índice en parent_id, cada
  nivel se convierte en un full table scan.
En SQL Server, usá OPTION (MAXRECURSION N) para anular el límite default de 100.
Construí una columna path para debugging, así podés ver la ruta exacta de recorrido.
CONNECT BY es la sintaxis propietaria de Oracle, también soportada por Snowflake.
Usar UNION en lugar de UNION ALL.
En SQL Server, usá OPTION (MAXRECURSION N).
Siempre incluí una columna depth o level.
Indexá parent_id e id; el join recursivo golpea esas columnas repetidamente.

Evitá la CTE recursiva para queries planas que no recorran una jerarquía; una CTE regular o un subquery es más
simple.

Agregá un depth limit como WHERE depth < 100, o trackeá los nodos visitados en un array o string de path y
verificá repeticiones.

PostgreSQL, MySQL 8.0+, SQLite 3.8.4+, SQL Server (2008+), Oracle (11gR2+), Snowflake, BigQuery y DuckDB las
soportan.

Las CTEs recursivas no soportan detección de ciclos de forma nativa, así que tenés
que construirla a mano.
Usá una CTE recursiva cuando necesitás recorrer una jerarquía desde un punto de partida conocido.
Las CTEs recursivas retornan depth-first por default.
Agregá un safety limit como WHERE depth < N para prevenir recursión infinita en datos cíclicos.
